lead.en: Osei Tutu unites the Ashanti under the Golden Stool

summary.en: Osei Tutu united the Asante states around Kumasi and defeated their former overlords, Denkyira. The Golden Stool became the symbol of unity, and the Ashanti Empire grew rich on the gold and slave trades.

lead.en: Peter the Great founds a new capital, a window on Europe

summary.en: During the Great Northern War, Peter I laid a fortress at the mouth of the Neva on land taken from Sweden. The new city became Russia's capital and its 'window on Europe', the emblem of Peter's reforms.

lead.en: Pirates run the Bahamas for a decade with no king

summary.en: In the early 1700s pirates took over New Providence island, home to Blackbeard, Charles Vane, Anne Bonny and hundreds more. Order rested on pirate articles, and captains were elected. In 1718 Governor Woodes Rogers arrived offering royal pardons, and the republic collapsed.

lead.en: Russia replaces Sweden as a great power

summary.en: Peter I's Russian army crushed the Swedish forces of Charles XII, who fled to the Ottoman Empire. The victory turned the Great Northern War: Sweden lost its great-power status and Russia gained it.

lead.en: Europe's harshest winter in 500 years weakens Sweden for Poltava

summary.en: The winter of 1708–09 was Europe's coldest in 500 years: Venice's canals and North Sea coasts froze, and famine struck France. Charles XII's army lost thousands of men to frost in Ukraine and arrived weakened at the Battle of Poltava.

lead.en: Peter I opens his cabinet of 'natural rarities' to the public

summary.en: In 1714 Peter I put his 'natural and human curiosities and rarities' on show in the Summer Palace, creating Russia's first public museum. He later bought the famous Dutch collections of Ruysch and Seba, and in 1727 the museum moved into its towered building on Vasilievsky Island.

title.en: The Amber Room, a gift to Peter I

lead.en: An 'eighth wonder' given for an alliance, then lost in war

summary.en: The amber panels were made for the Prussian king, but in 1716 Frederick William I gave them to Peter I to seal an alliance against Sweden. In 1941 the Nazis took the room to Königsberg and its fate is still unknown. A replica took 24 years and opened in the Catherine Palace in 2003.

lead.en: The fiercest pirate holds a city hostage for a medicine chest

summary.en: In May 1718 Edward Teach, known as Blackbeard, blockaded the port of Charleston for about a week, seizing ships and hostages. For ransom he demanded not gold but a chest of medicines — and got it. Six months later he was killed in a fight off Ocracoke Island.

lead.en: Istanbul's elite falls in love with tulips and garden parties

summary.en: Under Sultan Ahmed III the court embraced European fashions, Bosphorus palaces and tulips, paying fortunes for bulbs. The first Ottoman Turkish printing press appeared in these years. The era ended with the Patrona Halil revolt of 1730, which toppled the sultan.

lead.en: Long before the British, Aboriginal people traded with Asia

summary.en: From the 1720s at the latest (perhaps much earlier) fleets of sailing boats from Makassar on Sulawesi came each season to Australia's northern coast for trepang, sea cucumbers for the Chinese market. The Yolngu and other Aboriginal peoples of Arnhem Land worked with the Makassans and adopted words, dugout canoes and tobacco. The trade ended in 1907, when the Australian authorities stopped issuing licences.

lead.en: Isaac Newton loses a fortune in a stock bubble

summary.en: Between January and August 1720 South Sea Company shares soared from £128 to £1,000, then crashed, ruining thousands. Among the losers was Isaac Newton, said to have lost about £20,000. The episode helped make "bubble" the word for a speculative mania.

lead.en: Victory over Sweden makes Peter the Great an emperor

summary.en: After victory in the Great Northern War and the Treaty of Nystad with Sweden, the Senate proclaimed Peter I emperor in November 1721. Russia became an empire and a major European power with access to the Baltic.

lead.en: An Afghan army brings down the Safavid state

summary.en: In March 1722 the Ghilzai Afghans of Mahmud Hotak defeated the shah's army at Gulnabad and besieged Isfahan, the Safavid capital and one of the largest cities in the world. During the seven-month siege, by various accounts up to 80,000 inhabitants died of hunger and disease; in October Shah Soltan Hoseyn surrendered and crowned Mahmud himself. Russia and the Ottomans exploited Iran's weakness until Nader Shah restored order.

lead.en: Europeans first see the moai, on Easter Sunday

summary.en: On 5 April 1722, Easter Sunday, Jacob Roggeveen's Dutch expedition came upon a remote island in the eastern Pacific and named it Easter Island. The sailors described huge stone statues still standing on their platforms and, by their reckoning, several thousand inhabitants; during the landing the Dutch shot about a dozen islanders. The next Europeans did not arrive until 1770.

title.en: Founding of the Academy of Sciences

lead.en: Peter I creates a home for Euler, Bernoulli and Lomonosov

summary.en: In 1724 Peter I decreed the founding of the Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences, which opened in 1725. Its members included Leonhard Euler, Daniel Bernoulli and later Mikhail Lomonosov.

lead.en: The first of the states born of the Fula jihads

summary.en: Around 1725 (or 1727 by other accounts) the Muslim Fula of the Futa Jallon highlands, led by Karamoko Alfa, launched a holy war against their non-Muslim neighbours and local rulers. An imamate arose with its capital at Timbo and a council of notables; captives taken in raids were sold to Europeans on the coast. Futa Jallon inspired later jihads in Futa Toro and, in the 19th century, in Sokoto and Massina.

lead.en: A woman convinces royal surgeons she is giving birth to rabbits

summary.en: In autumn 1726 Mary Toft of Godalming appeared to give birth to rabbits, and several doctors, including a surgeon to the royal household, believed her. Brought to London and watched closely, she confessed to inserting the animals herself, and all England laughed at the gullible physicians.

lead.en: An inland kingdom seizes the coast and the slave trade

summary.en: King Agaja of Dahomey conquered Allada in 1724 and the port of Ouidah in 1727, gaining direct access to European slave traders. Ouidah became one of Africa's largest slave ports, and Dahomey a formidable military power famous for its female regiments, the Agojie. The kingdom lasted until the French conquest of 1894.

title.en: Müteferrika's first Ottoman Turkish printing press

lead.en: The first Ottoman Turkish press, 270 years after Gutenberg

summary.en: During the Tulip Era, the Hungarian-born convert İbrahim Müteferrika won Sultan Ahmed III's permission and a fatwa to print secular books in Arabic script. The first, Vankulu's dictionary, came out in 1729. By his death in 1745 he had issued 17 titles on history, geography and language, with his own maps and engravings.

lead.en: Bering maps Siberia's Arctic coast and reaches America

summary.en: In 1733–1743 an expedition led by Vitus Bering mapped Siberia's Arctic coast and the Kuril Islands. In 1741 the ships of Bering and Chirikov reached the coast of north-western America.

lead.en: Bach writes a comic piece about coffee addiction

summary.en: Bach wrote the Coffee Cantata for the student orchestra that played at Zimmermann’s coffee house in Leipzig. A father threatens to deny his daughter a husband unless she quits coffee; she sings it is sweeter than a thousand kisses.

lead.en: The world's largest bell has never rung once

summary.en: In 1735 Mikhail Motorin cast a bell of about 202 tonnes in the Kremlin. It was still in its casting pit when fire broke out in 1737: guards threw cold water on the hot bronze and a slab of over 10 tonnes cracked off. It has never been rung.

lead.en: The Peacock Throne goes to Iran as Mughal power wanes

summary.en: Iran's ruler Nader Shah defeated the Mughal army at Karnal and took Delhi, where his troops carried out a massacre. Enormous treasure, including the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, went to Iran; the Mughal Empire never recovered.

lead.en: Britain fights Spain over a sea captain's severed ear

summary.en: In 1731 a Spanish coast guard cut off the ear of British captain Robert Jenkins. Seven years later he reportedly displayed the pickled ear in Parliament, and in 1739 Britain declared war on Spain. Its first big success was the capture of Porto Bello in Panama.

lead.en: A mechanical duck that ate grain and 'digested' it

summary.en: Jacques de Vaucanson showed off a gilded duck that quacked, pecked at grain and soon produced droppings. Parisians believed it had an artificial digestive system; in fact the droppings were preloaded in a hidden compartment.

lead.en: Palace, furniture, cannons and an elephant — all made of ice

summary.en: In the winter of 1740 a 16-metre house was built of ice on the Neva, with ice furniture, a bed, logs in the fireplace, ice cannons and a life-size ice elephant. For sport the empress held a mock wedding there for Prince Golitsyn, and the couple had to spend the night on an ice bed.

lead.en: A celebrity rhino tours Europe for 17 years

summary.en: In 1741 a Dutch captain brought Clara the rhinoceros from India and toured her around Europe for 17 years in a huge carriage. Kings came to see her, artists painted her, and Paris ladies wore their hair à la rhinocéros.

lead.en: An emir and a preacher create the first Saudi state

summary.en: Emir Muhammad ibn Saud allied with the preacher Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. This pact of political power and strict religious doctrine created the first Saudi state, forerunner of modern Saudi Arabia.

lead.en: A tsunami wiped out Peru's main port

summary.en: On 28 October 1746 an earthquake of estimated magnitude 8.6–8.8 destroyed much of Lima, capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru. Soon afterwards a tsunami struck the port of Callao: of its roughly 5,000 inhabitants, by various accounts only about 200 survived. Lima was rebuilt with lower houses and lighter upper storeys, and the disaster ranks among the most severe in South American history.

title.en: Ahmad Shah Durrani founds the Afghan state

lead.en: Tribal elders pick a 25-year-old shah — and Afghanistan is born

summary.en: After Nader Shah's assassination, Pashtun chiefs met in a jirga near Kandahar and chose the young commander Ahmad Abdali as shah; he took the name Durrani, “pearl of pearls”. His realm stretched from Khorasan to Kashmir and the Punjab. Afghans honour him as Ahmad Shah Baba, the “father of the nation”.

lead.en: A compendium of knowledge becomes the Enlightenment's landmark

summary.en: Edited by Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert, the multi-volume Encyclopédie of sciences, arts and trades began to appear. Despite censorship and bans, it became the great monument of the Enlightenment, spreading ideas of reason and tolerance.

lead.en: Lightning is the same thing as a Leyden jar's spark

summary.en: In the summer of 1752, by his own account, Benjamin Franklin flew a kite with a metal point into a thunderstorm and drew a spark from a key on the wet string. It showed that lightning is electricity and made his lightning rod famous.

lead.en: A new Spanish–Portuguese border dooms the Jesuit missions

summary.en: Under the Treaty of Madrid of 1750 Spain ceded to Portugal seven Jesuit mission towns east of the Uruguay River in exchange for the colony of Sacramento. Some 30,000 Guaraní refused to leave their land; in 1756 a joint Spanish–Portuguese army crushed them at Caibaté, where by various estimates about 1,500 were killed. The war hastened the expulsion of the Jesuits from Portuguese territory in 1759.

lead.en: The ruin of Portugal's capital shakes Enlightenment thinkers

summary.en: On All Saints' Day 1755 an earthquake, tsunami and fires destroyed much of Lisbon, killing an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 people. The disaster shook Enlightenment thinkers; Voltaire responded with a poem and later with Candide.

lead.en: The last great nomad empire of Asia is destroyed

summary.en: In 1755 a Qing army occupied the Dzungar Khanate of the Oirats, weakened by internal strife, and after Amursana's revolt the Qianlong Emperor ordered the Dzungars exterminated. Historians estimate that some 70–80% of roughly 500,000–600,000 people died from massacre, famine and smallpox, while others fled to Russia and the Kazakh steppe. The Qing resettled the emptied land with people from elsewhere, and it later became the province of Xinjiang.

lead.en: Lomonosov and Shuvalov open higher learning to many classes

summary.en: In January 1755 Empress Elizabeth signed the decree founding Moscow University, based on a plan by Mikhail Lomonosov and Ivan Shuvalov. It became Russia's first university open to students of various classes.

lead.en: A global war before the world wars wins Britain Canada

summary.en: Britain and Prussia fought France, Austria and Russia on several continents, in what is often called the first truly global war. Britain took Canada from France and strengthened its hold on India, while Frederick II's Prussia kept Silesia.

lead.en: The Company takes Bengal, beginning British rule in India

summary.en: East India Company forces under Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal, whose commander Mir Jafar defected to the British. The Company gained control of Bengal, the start of British rule in India.

title.en: Battle of the Plains of Abraham

lead.en: Britain takes Quebec, and France loses Canada

summary.en: In the Seven Years' War, General Wolfe's British troops defeated the Marquis de Montcalm's French outside Quebec; both commanders were killed. By the 1763 Treaty of Paris, France ceded Canada to Britain.

lead.en: Machines replace hand labor and remake how the world lives

summary.en: In Britain handwork began to give way to machines: spinning frames, the steam engine and coke-smelted iron. Factory production and urban growth transformed the economy, society and daily life first of Europe and then of the whole world.

lead.en: The Maratha defeat clears the way for the British in India

summary.en: On 14 January 1761 the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani and his Indian allies crushed the Maratha army commanded by Sadashivrao Bhau. It was one of the largest battles of the 18th century: estimates of those killed in the fighting and the massacres that followed range from 60,000 to 100,000. Maratha power was weakened for a decade, the Durranis did not hold northern India, and the British East India Company filled the vacuum.

lead.en: The guards depose Peter III, opening Catherine's 34-year reign

summary.en: In July 1762 the guards overthrew Emperor Peter III and placed his wife Catherine on the throne. During her 34-year reign Russia expanded south and west, and reforms were pursued in the spirit of the Enlightenment.

lead.en: Catherine II buys 225 paintings, founding a great museum

summary.en: In 1764 Catherine II bought a collection of 225 paintings from the Berlin merchant Gotzkowsky. This is regarded as the founding of the Hermitage, at first the empress's private collection, opened to the public in 1852.

lead.en: Burma burns Siam's capital; power shifts to Bangkok

summary.en: After a long siege, the Burmese army took and burned Ayutthaya, capital of Siam and one of Asia's richest cities. The kingdom was soon restored by Taksin, and in 1782 the capital moved to Bangkok.

lead.en: Cook charts New Zealand and claims eastern Australia

summary.en: Aboard HMS Endeavour, James Cook observed the transit of Venus in Tahiti, charted New Zealand and in 1770 landed at Botany Bay. He claimed Australia's east coast for the British Crown.

lead.en: A giant of northern seas is gone 27 years after its discovery

summary.en: Georg Steller described this giant sea cow, up to 8 m long, during Bering's expedition in 1741. Fur hunters killed it for meat, and by the generally accepted estimate it was gone by 1768, just 27 years after discovery, early in Catherine II's reign.

lead.en: An efficient engine drives the Industrial Revolution

summary.en: Scottish engineer James Watt patented a steam engine with a separate condenser, far more efficient than earlier designs. Watt's improved engines powered Britain's Industrial Revolution.

lead.en: A Polynesian drew Cook a map of the Pacific from memory

summary.en: The priest and navigator Tupaia of Raiatea joined the Endeavour at Tahiti in 1769. From his knowledge a chart was drawn showing dozens of islands across thousands of kilometres, a digest of Polynesian wayfinding. In New Zealand he served as interpreter, since Māori understood his language, and many took him, not Cook, for the expedition's leader. He died in Batavia in 1770.

lead.en: Emperors reign but do not rule as warlords carve up the land

summary.en: In 1769 Ras Mikael Sehul of Tigray had Emperor Iyoas I killed and turned the throne at Gondar into a plaything of the nobility. For nearly ninety years Ethiopia was in effect ruled by rival regional lords, the rases, while emperors, sometimes replaced several times a year, were puppets. The era ended in 1855, when Tewodros II reunited the country by force.

title.en: Cugnot's steam wagon, the first car

lead.en: The first self-propelled car was built to haul cannons

summary.en: Army engineer Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot built a three-wheeled steam wagon to haul artillery for the French army. It moved at walking pace, kept stopping to raise steam and, legend has it, once crashed into a wall.

lead.en: A chess machine plays Napoleon — with a man hidden inside

summary.en: In 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen showed Empress Maria Theresa a chess-playing automaton dressed as a Turk. For 84 years it toured Europe and America, beating opponents including Napoleon and Benjamin Franklin. The secret was a strong chess player hidden inside the cabinet.

lead.en: A teenage Mozart transcribes the Vatican's secret music by ear

summary.en: Gregorio Allegri's Miserere was sung in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week, and copying the score was forbidden. In 1770, as his father told it, 14-year-old Mozart heard it once and wrote it all down from memory. Soon after, the pope made him a knight of the Golden Spur.

title.en: The Thunder Stone reaches Saint Petersburg

lead.en: The largest stone ever moved by human beings

summary.en: For the Bronze Horseman's pedestal a granite boulder of some 1,500 tonnes was found at Lakhta. It took almost two years to drag it overland and float it on a purpose-built barge to the city in 1770 — the largest stone ever moved by humans. The monument was unveiled in 1782.

lead.en: Three village brothers topple rulers and rout a Qing army

summary.en: In 1771 three brothers from the village of Tây Sơn in central Vietnam rose against official abuses. Within two decades they crushed the southern Nguyễn lords and the northern Trịnh, ended the Lê dynasty, and in 1789 the youngest, Nguyễn Huệ (Emperor Quang Trung), routed a Qing army near Thăng Long. After his death in 1792 Nguyễn Ánh struck back and in 1802 united the country under the Nguyễn dynasty.

lead.en: Three neighbors carve up the state until Poland vanishes

summary.en: In 1772, 1793 and 1795 Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth among themselves. The state vanished from the map; Russia gained Lithuania, Belarus and right-bank Ukraine.

lead.en: A Cossack claims to be Peter III and raises the Volga and Urals

summary.en: Don Cossack Yemelyan Pugachev, claiming to be Emperor Peter III, raised the Yaik Cossacks, joined by serfs, factory workers and peoples of the Volga and Urals. The largest revolt of Catherine II's reign was crushed and Pugachev executed in Moscow.

lead.en: The rider who never shouted 'The British are coming!'

summary.en: On the night of 18 April 1775 the silversmith Paul Revere rode out to warn the militia that British troops were moving. He did not shout 'The British are coming!': the mission was secret, and colonists still thought of themselves as British.

lead.en: Thirteen colonies declare freedom and the rights of man

summary.en: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration drafted by Thomas Jefferson, proclaiming the thirteen colonies independent of Britain. Its words on equality and unalienable rights inspired revolutions around the world.

lead.en: Europe's encounter with Hawaii turns to bloodshed

summary.en: In January 1779 Cook's ships entered Kealakekua Bay, where they were received with honours during the Makahiki festival. Returning weeks later with a broken mast, the British quarrelled with the Hawaiians; on 14 February Cook tried to take the paramount chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage over a stolen boat and was killed on the shore with four marines. His third voyage opened Hawaii to Europe.

lead.en: The largest uprising against Spanish rule in the Americas

summary.en: Cacique José Gabriel Condorcanqui, taking the name of the last Inca ruler Túpac Amaru, led the indigenous people of Peru against colonial oppression. The largest revolt in Spanish America was crushed and its leader executed in Cusco.

lead.en: A prisoner makes a toothbrush from a dinner bone

summary.en: Jailed in Newgate in 1770 for rioting, William Addis drilled holes in a bone saved from dinner and tied in bristles. Once free he started making toothbrushes, and by 1780 they were mass-produced.

lead.en: The start of the Chakri dynasty, still reigning in Thailand

summary.en: In 1782 the general Chao Phraya Chakri took the throne as Rama I and moved the capital to the east bank of the Chao Phraya river. There the Grand Palace and the Temple of the Emerald Buddha rose. The new city's ceremonial name is one of the longest place names in the world, and the Chakri dynasty founded then still reigns in Thailand.

title.en: Execution of Anna Göldi, Europe's 'last witch'

lead.en: A maid beheaded for witchcraft in the Age of Reason

summary.en: Anna Göldi, a maid, was accused of bewitching her employer's daughter and confessed under torture. She was beheaded in Glarus in 1782; the trial outraged enlightened Europe, and in 2008 the canton declared her innocent.

lead.en: The book where 'let them eat brioche' first appears

summary.en: Jean-Jacques Rousseau's autobiography appeared after his death, in 1782. In it he recalls 'a great princess' telling breadless peasants to eat brioche — lines written around 1765, when Marie Antoinette was nine.

lead.en: Toxic gases kill a fifth of Iceland and veil Europe in haze

summary.en: For eight months the Laki fissure poured out lava and toxic gases. Most livestock died, and famine killed about a fifth of Iceland's people. A sulphurous haze spread over Europe, bringing a scorching summer and a bitter winter. That year, Russia annexed Crimea.

lead.en: The khanate passes to Russia and Sevastopol is founded

summary.en: On 19 April 1783 Catherine II's manifesto annexed the Crimean Khanate after the abdication of Khan Şahin Giray. Sevastopol, base of the Black Sea Fleet, was founded the same year.

lead.en: For the first time, people rise into the sky

summary.en: On 21 November 1783 Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes rose over Paris in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon, flying about 9 km in 25 minutes. It was the first free flight by humans.

lead.en: A pharmacist wins the French over to potatoes

summary.en: Parmentier came to love potatoes as a prisoner in Prussia and promoted them ever after. Louis XVI gave him a field near Paris; legend says soldiers guarded it by day and left at night so the curious could steal the tubers.

lead.en: Separation of powers in the oldest written constitution in force

summary.en: The Philadelphia Convention, chaired by George Washington, signed a Constitution creating a federal republic with separation of powers. In force since 1789, it is the oldest written national constitution still in use.

title.en: Catherine's Crimean journey and the 'Potemkin villages'

lead.en: The famous fake villages were most likely a rumour

summary.en: In 1787 Catherine II spent six months touring New Russia and Crimea with foreign envoys. The tale of fake villages Potemkin supposedly moved along her route came from the Saxon diplomat Helbig, who was not on the trip. Historians call it a myth: Potemkin decorated real towns, openly.

lead.en: Ships of convicts begin the British settlement of Australia

summary.en: Eleven British ships under Captain Arthur Phillip brought over a thousand people, mostly convicts, to Sydney Cove. The colony of New South Wales, founded on 26 January, began the British colonisation of Australia.

lead.en: A symbol of absolutism falls and the French Revolution begins

summary.en: On 14 July, insurgent Parisians stormed the Bastille, a fortress-prison and symbol of royal absolutism. It marked the start of the French Revolution, which proclaimed liberty, equality and the rights of man.

title.en: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

lead.en: “Men are born and remain free and equal in rights”

summary.en: On 26 August 1789 France's National Constituent Assembly adopted a declaration of natural rights: liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression, equality before the law and the sovereignty of the nation. It underpinned French constitutions and became a model for declarations of rights around the world.

lead.en: Sailors mutiny aboard a ship carrying breadfruit trees

summary.en: The Bounty was carrying breadfruit seedlings from Tahiti to the West Indies when in April 1789 Fletcher Christian led a mutiny. Captain Bligh and 18 loyal men were set adrift in a launch, which Bligh sailed 6,700 km to Timor. The mutineers hid on Pitcairn, where their descendants still live.

lead.en: America's first president had one tooth of his own left

summary.en: On 30 April 1789 Washington took the oath as first US president in New York. By then he had a single tooth of his own left; his dentures were made of hippopotamus ivory, metal and human teeth — never wood.

lead.en: Former slaves win and build their own independent nation

summary.en: A slave uprising in the French colony of Saint-Domingue grew into a revolution led by Toussaint Louverture. In 1804 Haiti was proclaimed, the first state founded by former slaves and the first independent nation in Latin America.

lead.en: Modern Europe's first written national constitution

summary.en: On 3 May 1791 the Great Sejm adopted a constitution for the Commonwealth, Europe's first modern codified constitution. It abolished the liberum veto but was overturned after Russian intervention in 1792.

lead.en: Salieri didn't poison him — he later taught his son

summary.en: Mozart died in Vienna on 5 December 1791, aged 35, most likely of illness. The rumour that Salieri poisoned him was made famous by Pushkin's play, though Salieri went on to teach Mozart's younger son.

lead.en: A 'free town' for ex-slaves who fought for the British Crown

summary.en: In 1792 some 1,100 Black Loyalists, former slaves who had fought for Britain in the American War of Independence, sailed from Nova Scotia on 15 ships and founded Freetown. After the slave trade was banned in 1807, the Royal Navy landed Africans freed from slave ships here. From this mix arose the Krio people and their language.

lead.en: Named after a doctor who opposed the death penalty

summary.en: The guillotine was first used in Paris on 25 April 1792. Dr Guillotin did not invent it: he merely proposed one quick method for all, and the machine, modelled on older devices, was designed by the surgeon Antoine Louis and built by Tobias Schmidt.

lead.en: Qianlong turns down Britain's bid for wider trade

summary.en: British envoy Lord Macartney was received by the Qianlong Emperor at his summer retreat, but all requests for wider trade and a permanent embassy were refused. The rebuff revealed the gulf between China and the West before the Opium Wars.

lead.en: Ten hours a day, 100 minutes an hour: France remakes time

summary.en: Along with the metre, revolutionary France brought in decimal time: ten hours a day, 100 minutes an hour, 100 seconds a minute. Clockmakers built ten-hour dials, but habit won, and the requirement was dropped within two years.

title.en: The iron maiden legend is born

lead.en: A 'medieval' torture device invented in the 18th century

summary.en: In 1793 the German philosopher Johann Siebenkees described an execution in an 'iron maiden' at Nuremberg in 1515, without reliable sources. The famous museum specimens were assembled in the 19th century from unrelated old artefacts.

title.en: Cavalry captures a fleet at Den Helder

lead.en: Hussars capture a warfleet frozen in the ice

summary.en: In the harsh winter of 1795 the Dutch fleet was frozen in at Den Helder. On the night of 23 January French hussars approached across the ice, and 14 warships surrendered without a fight — one of the rare times in history that cavalry captured a fleet.

lead.en: Cowpox shields against smallpox — vaccination is born

summary.en: In May 1796 country doctor Edward Jenner inoculated young James Phipps with cowpox and showed it protected against smallpox. Vaccination was born — a method that saved hundreds of millions of lives and later made smallpox eradication possible.

lead.en: Napoleon takes Cairo, and Egyptology is born

summary.en: Napoleon Bonaparte's army routed Murad Bey's Mamluk cavalry and occupied Cairo. The scholars who accompanied the campaign, and the Rosetta Stone found by its soldiers, launched Egyptology and paved the way for growing European influence in the Middle East.

lead.en: For the first time, current flows through a wire steadily

summary.en: Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked card and got a steady current. He reported the battery to the Royal Society in London in 1800; the unit of voltage, the volt, is named after him.

lead.en: Cossacks sent to conquer India with maps that end at Khiva

summary.en: In January 1801 Paul I ordered Ataman Orlov's Don Cossacks to march via Bukhara and Khiva to the Indus and strike British India. Some 20,000 Cossacks rode into the steppe; Paul's orders admitted his maps went only as far as Khiva and the rest was their affair. News of his murder in March turned them back.

lead.en: The US doubled in size for $15 million

summary.en: President Jefferson wanted to buy only New Orleans from France, but Napoleon, short of money for his war with Britain, offered all of Louisiana. For $15 million the US gained some 2.1 million km² between the Mississippi and the Rocky Mountains, nearly doubling the country. In 1804 the Lewis and Clark expedition set out to explore the new lands as far as the Pacific.

lead.en: Napoleon crowns himself and the Republic becomes an Empire

summary.en: In the presence of Pope Pius VII, Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself emperor and then crowned Josephine. The French Republic became an empire, and over the next decade Napoleon redrew the map of Europe.

lead.en: Karađorđe leads the Serbs against Ottoman rule

summary.en: In 1804 Serbs led by Karađorđe rose against the Janissaries and then against the Ottoman Empire. Crushed in 1813, the uprising began the struggle that led to Serbian independence.

title.en: Usman dan Fodio's jihad and the Sokoto Caliphate

lead.en: A Fulani preacher builds West Africa's largest state

summary.en: In 1804 the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio declared jihad on the rulers of the Hausa cities, accusing them of extortion and straying from Islam. Within a few years his followers had united more than 30 emirates into the Sokoto Caliphate, one of 19th-century Africa's largest states. Britain conquered it in 1903, but the Sultan of Sokoto remains the spiritual leader of Nigeria's Muslims.

lead.en: Former slaves found a nation of their own

summary.en: On 1 January 1804 Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared the former French colony of Saint-Domingue independent. Haiti became the first state born of a successful slave revolt and the second independent nation in the Americas.

lead.en: A medical student drank patients' vomit to prove a point

summary.en: A University of Pennsylvania student was sure yellow fever was not contagious. He rubbed patients' vomit into cuts, dripped it in his eyes and drank it, and never fell ill. He was wrong anyway: mosquitoes carry the disease, as was proved nearly a century later.

title.en: Muhammad Ali becomes ruler of Egypt

lead.en: An Albanian officer turns Egypt into a regional power

summary.en: In 1805 Muhammad Ali, commander of an Albanian unit of the Ottoman army, became governor of Egypt. In 1811 he massacred the Mamluk elite at a feast in the Cairo Citadel, then launched a modernisation drive: factories, cotton, a European-style army, students sent to France. His dynasty ruled Egypt until the revolution of 1952.

lead.en: Nelson crushes the Franco-Spanish fleet and dies in battle

summary.en: On 21 October 1805 Admiral Nelson's British fleet destroyed the combined Franco-Spanish fleet off Cape Trafalgar. Nelson was mortally wounded, but the victory secured British command of the seas for a century and ended Napoleon's plans to invade England.

lead.en: The Don Cossacks move their flood-prone capital to a hill

summary.en: The old Cossack capital of Cherkassk flooded every spring, so in 1805 Ataman Matvei Platov founded a new town on a high hill. Novocherkassk became the capital of the Don Cossack Host and remained so until 1920.

lead.en: European guns shattered the old balance between the tribes

summary.en: Once Māori began trading for European muskets, old tribal feuds turned into a devastating arms race. The Ngāpuhi chief Hongi Hika visited England in 1820 and came back with hundreds of guns to strike his neighbours. Over three decades hundreds of battles were fought; by various estimates 20,000 to 40,000 people died, and whole tribes were driven from their lands.

title.en: Rio becomes the capital of Portugal

lead.en: For 13 years a colony is the capital of its own empire

summary.en: Fleeing Napoleon's army, the Portuguese court boarded ships at the end of 1807 and sailed to Brazil. From 1808 to 1821 Rio de Janeiro was the capital of the whole Portuguese empire, a rare case of a colony governing its mother country.

lead.en: Bolívar and San Martín free most of a continent

summary.en: Exploiting the crisis of the Spanish monarchy, the American colonies rose for independence. Armies led by Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín liberated most of the continent; the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824 proved decisive.

lead.en: Rival islands merge into a kingdom that lasts until 1893

summary.en: After years of war the chief Kamehameha conquered the islands, and in 1810 the ruler of Kauaʻi accepted his rule. The Kingdom of Hawaii he founded lasted until American planters overthrew the monarchy in 1893.

lead.en: A confectioner wins Napoleon’s prize for preserving food

summary.en: France offered 12,000 francs for a way to preserve food for its army and navy. In 1810 the confectioner Nicolas Appert won it by heating food in sealed bottles, without knowing why it kept.

lead.en: The Grande Armée takes Moscow, then perishes in retreat

summary.en: In June 1812 Napoleon's Grande Armée crossed the Neman. After the Battle of Borodino the French took Moscow but, failing to force peace, retreated, and by year's end the army was almost destroyed. The campaign turned the tide of the Napoleonic Wars.

title.en: Fort Ross, Russia's outpost in California

lead.en: Russians build California's first windmills and ships

summary.en: In 1812 Ivan Kuskov with 25 Russians and 80 Native Alaskans founded Fort Ross north of San Francisco, the southernmost settlement of Russian America. It had California's first windmills and shipyards. In 1841 it was sold to John Sutter, at whose mill gold was later found.

lead.en: The capital of the Talysh Khanate passes to Russia

summary.en: During the Russo-Persian War, General Kotlyarevsky's force stormed Lankaran, the Persian-held fortress of the Talysh Khanate, on 1 January 1813. That October the Treaty of Gulistan gave Talysh to Russia; today the Talysh homeland is split between Azerbaijan and Iran.

lead.en: Napoleon's victors redraw the map of Europe for decades

summary.en: From September 1814 to June 1815 the European powers, led by Metternich, Alexander I, Castlereagh and Talleyrand, negotiated the post-war order. The Congress restored monarchies, created the German Confederation and a Kingdom of Poland under the Russian emperor, and founded the “Concert of Europe” that kept the continent from a general war until 1914.

lead.en: A wave of porter bursts a brewery wall and floods a slum

summary.en: On 17 October 1814 a 22-foot vat of porter burst at a London brewery, knocking open another; between 580,000 and 1.5 million litres of beer poured out. The wave flattened the brewery's back wall and swept into the St Giles slum, killing eight people.

lead.en: The mightiest blast in recorded history cools the whole planet

summary.en: In April 1815 Tambora produced the most powerful eruption in recorded history: the mountain lost over a kilometre of height and an estimated 70,000+ people died. Its stratospheric ash cooled the planet. Two months later, Napoleon lost at Waterloo.

lead.en: Wellington and Blücher end the Napoleonic era

summary.en: On 18 June 1815 Wellington's allied army and Blücher's Prussians defeated Napoleon. The battle ended the Hundred Days and the Napoleonic Wars, while the Congress of Vienna set up a new order in Europe.

lead.en: July snow, failed harvests — and the birth of Frankenstein

summary.en: After Tambora, snow fell in New England in summer 1816 and harvests failed across Europe, bringing famine. Kept indoors by storms at the Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva, Mary Shelley and Lord Byron held a ghost-story contest that gave birth to Frankenstein.

lead.en: New battle tactics unleash the upheaval of the Mfecane

summary.en: Shaka became chief of the Zulu, remodelled the army around short spears and the 'horns of the buffalo' tactic, and subdued neighbouring peoples. His conquests set off a wave of wars and migrations across southern Africa known as the Mfecane.

lead.en: A Ganges delta disease follows trade routes all the way to Russia

summary.en: In 1817 cholera, long endemic to the Ganges delta, broke out along trade routes and with British troops. It swept South and Southeast Asia and the Middle East, reaching Astrakhan in Russia by 1823. It was the first of seven cholera pandemics.

title.en: San Martín's Crossing of the Andes

lead.en: An army crossed mountains higher than the Alps to free Chile

place.en: Andean passes between Argentina and Chile

summary.en: In January 1817 General José de San Martín led the Army of the Andes, about five thousand men, from Mendoza in Argentina over passes higher than 3,500 metres. Cold and altitude killed many men and most of the horses and mules. But the Spanish were caught off guard: on 12 February the patriots won at Chacabuco, opening the way to independence for Chile and then Peru.

title.en: Drais's dandy horse, the first bicycle

lead.en: The first bicycle had no pedals: you pushed with your feet

summary.en: In 1817 Baron Karl Drais built a two-wheeled 'running machine', the first bicycle. It had no pedals: the rider pushed off the ground and on a level road reached about 16 km/h, twice walking pace. The English nicknamed it the dandy horse.

lead.en: An adventurer raises the Russian flag over Kauai

summary.en: Georg Schäffer, a German doctor working for the Russian-American Company, persuaded Kauai's chief Kaumualiʻi to accept Alexander I's protection and in 1817 built the stone Fort Elizabeth at Waimea under a Russian flag. The tsar had not asked for it, and by autumn the Hawaiians had expelled him.

lead.en: A fishing island becomes the Empire's free port

summary.en: In January 1819 Thomas Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company landed on a sparsely inhabited island off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. In February he signed a treaty with local rulers and founded a trading post. A duty-free port at the crossroads between India and China, it grew rapidly into one of the world's great harbours.

lead.en: Bellingshausen and Lazarev see the sixth continent

summary.en: On 28 January 1820 the sloops Vostok and Mirny under Fabian von Bellingshausen and Mikhail Lazarev approached the Antarctic ice shelf. It was among the first sightings of the sixth continent, whose existence had been only a hypothesis for centuries.

lead.en: The Portuguese king's own son freed the colony and became emperor

summary.en: On 7 September 1822, on the banks of the Ipiranga stream, Prince Regent Pedro, son of the King of Portugal, declared 'Independence or death!' He was soon crowned Emperor Pedro I. Unlike Spain's possessions, which split into many republics, vast Brazil stayed united and remained a monarchy until 1889.

lead.en: Stephenson's locomotive opens the railway age

summary.en: On 27 September 1825 the Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in England, the first public railway to use steam locomotives. The train was hauled by George Stephenson's Locomotion No. 1. The railway age that transformed industry and trade had begun.

lead.en: Officers demand a constitution on Senate Square

summary.en: On 26 December 1825 noble officers led troops onto Senate Square, refusing to swear allegiance to Nicholas I and demanding a constitution. The revolt was crushed by artillery; five leaders were hanged and over a hundred exiled to Siberia.

lead.en: Prince Diponegoro fights the Dutch for five years

summary.en: Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta rose against the Dutch colonial authorities and the nobles who backed them. The guerrilla war lasted five years and, by estimates, cost some 200,000 Javanese lives. In 1830 the prince was arrested during negotiations and exiled to Sulawesi, and the Dutch imposed the Cultivation System, enriching the Netherlands at Java's expense.

title.en: The first photograph: View from the Window at Le Gras

lead.en: The oldest photo needed hours, maybe days, of exposure

summary.en: Around 1827 Nicéphore Niépce photographed the rooftops outside his window, the oldest surviving camera photograph. The image formed on a bitumen-coated plate. Sunlight falls on buildings on both sides, so the exposure was put at eight hours; recent experiments suggest several days.

lead.en: Persia loses Erivan and Nakhchivan; the border moves to the Aras

summary.en: The treaty ended the Russo-Persian War of 1826–1828. Qajar Iran ceded the khanates of Erivan and Nakhchivan to Russia, paid 20 million silver rubles and granted Russian subjects extraterritorial rights. Alexander Griboyedov took part in the talks; a year later, as envoy, he was killed when a mob stormed the Russian mission in Tehran.

lead.en: A queen who kept Europe at bay for 33 years

summary.en: In 1828 the widow of King Radama I took the throne of Merina, the state that had united most of Madagascar. Ranavalona I expelled missionaries, banned Christianity and harshly persecuted converts, and repelled British and French naval attacks. Yet she used European skills: the Frenchman Jean Laborde built her an entire industrial complex. Europeans called her the 'mad queen'; Malagasy historians judge her more kindly.

lead.en: The most recognisable Japanese print in the world

summary.en: Around 1831 the seventy-year-old Katsushika Hokusai published the print series 'Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji'. It opened with a claw-crested wave towering over fishermen's boats, with a tiny Mount Fuji in the distance. Hokusai used a newly imported pigment, Prussian blue. The print ran to thousands of impressions and later inspired Van Gogh and Debussy.

title.en: Abolition of slavery in the British Empire

lead.en: Some 800,000 enslaved people are set free

summary.en: The British Parliament abolished slavery in almost all of the empire's colonies, freeing some 800,000 people, mostly in the West Indies. The act crowned a long abolitionist campaign and set an example for other nations.

lead.en: Pushkin, not Peter, coined the window to Europe — via an Italian

summary.en: In autumn 1833 at Boldino Pushkin wrote his poem about Peter and the Petersburg flood. He footnoted the line about cutting a window to Europe: the image came from the Italian Francesco Algarotti, who called Petersburg a window through which Russia looks at Europe.

lead.en: Thousands of Boers head inland in ox wagons

summary.en: From 1835, resenting British rule and the abolition of slavery, some 12,000–15,000 Dutch-speaking Boer settlers left the Cape Colony in ox wagons. They pushed into Ndebele and Zulu lands; in 1838 at Blood River they repelled a Zulu army. The trekkers founded the republics of Natalia, the Orange Free State and the Transvaal, the seedbed of later Afrikaner nationalism.

lead.en: Five weeks that set evolutionary theory in motion

summary.en: In September and October 1835 HMS Beagle spent about five weeks in the Galápagos, where the young naturalist Charles Darwin collected birds, plants and tortoises. He later noticed that mockingbirds and finches differed markedly from island to island. That puzzle helped lead him to natural selection, set out in 1859 in On the Origin of Species.

lead.en: A newspaper 'finds' unicorns and bat-men on the Moon

summary.en: In August 1835 New York's The Sun ran six articles claiming astronomer John Herschel had seen life on the Moon through a giant telescope: bison, unicorns, two-legged beavers and winged bat-men who built temples. Weeks later the paper admitted it was invented.

title.en: Premiere of A Life for the Tsar

lead.en: The opera behind the Susanin story we know

summary.en: Glinka's opera, staged in St Petersburg in 1836, turned the Kostroma peasant Ivan Susanin into a national hero. The tale of him leading Poles into the wilderness took shape in 19th-century literature; a 1619 charter says only that enemies tortured him to death.

lead.en: Trains take the public to concerts — and give Russia 'vokzal'

summary.en: On 30 October 1837 the first train ran from Saint Petersburg to Tsarskoye Selo in 35 minutes. The line carried almost no freight: its Pavlovsk terminus was built as a concert 'vauxhall' after London's pleasure gardens, which is why Russians still call a railway station a 'vokzal'.

lead.en: The Cherokee are marched over a thousand kilometres west

summary.en: Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, the 'Five Civilized Tribes' of the southeastern US were forced west of the Mississippi. In 1838–1839 soldiers drove about 16,000 Cherokee from their homeland, even though the Supreme Court had upheld their rights. By various estimates up to four thousand died on the way from disease, hunger and cold.

lead.en: France blockades Mexico over a looted pastry shop

summary.en: A French pastry chef, Remontel, complained to his king that Mexican officers had looted his shop and demanded 60,000 pesos, though it was worth under 1,000. In 1838 France, adding other claims, billed Mexico 600,000 pesos and blockaded its ports. The war took the baker's name.

lead.en: Britain takes Hong Kong as China's century of humiliation begins

summary.en: The war began after Qing officials tried to stop the British opium trade at Canton. China's defeat was sealed by the 1842 Treaty of Nanking: Britain gained Hong Kong and five ports opened to foreigners. It opened China's so-called century of humiliation.

lead.en: France gives the world a way to capture a moment

summary.en: In August 1839 Louis Daguerre's process for fixing images on silvered plates was made public at the French Academy of Sciences. The French government bought the invention and gave it to the world, and photography spread rapidly.

title.en: The Edict of Gülhane opens the Tanzimat

lead.en: An edict read in a rose garden promises equality to all subjects

summary.en: On 3 November 1839 the minister Mustafa Reşid Pasha read out the Edict of Gülhane on behalf of the young Sultan Abdulmejid I. It guaranteed subjects' life, honour and property regardless of religion and promised fair taxes and orderly conscription. It opened the Tanzimat — nearly 40 years of European-style reform of the army, schools, courts and laws.

lead.en: The retreat from Kabul: one of Britain's worst disasters in Asia

summary.en: Fearing Russian influence, Britain invaded Afghanistan in 1839 and installed the puppet Shah Shuja. A rising in Kabul forced the British to retreat over the winter passes in January 1842: a column of 4,500 troops and some 12,000 camp followers was almost entirely wiped out. Army surgeon William Brydon reached Jalalabad, and his arrival became the emblem of the disaster.

lead.en: New Zealand passes under the British Crown

summary.en: On 6 February 1840 representatives of the British Crown and Māori chiefs signed a treaty bringing New Zealand under British rule. The English and Māori texts differed in meaning, fuelling long disputes; the treaty is regarded as the country's founding document.

title.en: Penny Black, the first postage stamp

lead.en: For the first time, the sender pays for a letter in advance

summary.en: Until 1840 British letters were paid for by the recipient, by distance and number of sheets. Rowland Hill’s reform brought a flat penny rate and a stamp with the young Victoria’s profile.

lead.en: Ringing non-stop since 1840 on its original batteries

summary.en: In Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory a bell has been running on dry piles since 1840, ringing an estimated 10 billion times. You can't hear it through the glass, and no one knows exactly what the batteries contain, since nobody wants to open them.

lead.en: The fax machine came 33 years before the telephone

summary.en: In 1843 the Scottish clockmaker Alexander Bain received a British patent for an 'electric printing telegraph' in which pendulums at both ends of a wire swept line by line in step to copy an image. It was the forerunner of the fax machine, invented before the telephone.

lead.en: For the first time, news outruns the messenger

summary.en: On 24 May 1844 Samuel Morse sent the message "What hath God wrought" from the US Capitol to Baltimore. The electric telegraph let news travel faster than any messenger for the first time and soon wired whole continents together.

lead.en: Collectors pay for rarity — fishermen kill the final pair

summary.en: On 3 June 1844 fishermen on the Eldey stack off Iceland killed the last confirmed pair of great auks for a dealer, crushing their egg. The rarer the flightless bird became, the more collectors paid for its skins and eggs.

title.en: The Báb's declaration and the birth of Bábism

lead.en: A Shiraz merchant calls himself the “Gate” — Baháʼí roots

summary.en: On 23 May 1844 the young merchant Sayyid ʻAlí Muhammad declared himself the Báb, the “Gate” to the hidden imam. His movement spread fast across Iran and was harshly suppressed; the Báb himself was executed by firing squad in Tabriz in 1850. His follower Baháʼu'lláh, in Baghdad in 1863, founded a new religion — the Baháʼí Faith.

lead.en: Potato blight kills a million and drives a million abroad

summary.en: Potato blight, arriving from the Americas, destroyed the staple food of Ireland's poor year after year. About a million people died and another million emigrated, mostly to the United States. Ireland's population has never returned to its pre-famine level.

lead.en: Wars over land that cost the Māori their best territory

summary.en: In March 1845 warriors of the chief Hōne Heke felled the British flagstaff again and sacked Kororāreka. This opened wars between the colonial government and some Māori iwi; other Māori fought for the Crown. The largest was the Waikato campaign of 1863–64. Some 3,000 people died by most estimates, and confiscations stripped Māori of over a million hectares of land.

title.en: First public demonstration of ether anaesthesia

lead.en: Surgery without pain — modern operating begins

summary.en: On 16 October 1846 at Massachusetts General Hospital, dentist William Morton put a patient under with ether while a surgeon removed a tumour painlessly. Anaesthesia spread worldwide within months and made modern surgery possible.

lead.en: Mexico loses about half its territory

summary.en: After the US annexed Texas in 1845, a border dispute turned into war. In September 1847 American troops stormed Chapultepec Castle, where young cadets, the Niños Héroes still honoured in Mexico, fell, and entered Mexico City. Under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848 Mexico ceded California, New Mexico and other lands, about half its territory.

title.en: Neptune found 'with the tip of a pen'

lead.en: A planet calculated first, then found in a single night

summary.en: From the wobbles in Uranus's orbit, Urbain Le Verrier calculated where an unknown planet should be and wrote to Berlin. Johann Galle got the letter on 23 September 1846 and that same night found Neptune less than a degree from the predicted spot.

lead.en: Africa's first republic, founded by descendants of slaves

summary.en: From 1822 the American Colonization Society settled freed Black Americans on the West African coast. On 26 July 1847 the colony declared independence, with Virginia-born Joseph Jenkins Roberts as first president. Liberia became Africa's first republic, though for more than a century power stayed with the Americo-Liberian minority, sidelining indigenous peoples.

lead.en: Chocolate becomes something to eat, not just drink

summary.en: For nearly three centuries after Columbus, Europeans only drank chocolate. In 1847 the Bristol firm of Fry & Sons mixed cocoa powder, sugar and cocoa butter into a mould, creating the first bar meant for eating.

title.en: Semmelweis tells doctors to wash their hands

lead.en: Handwashing saved mothers, and his colleagues took offence

summary.en: In a Vienna hospital, mothers on the doctors' ward died of fever far more often than on the midwives'. Ignaz Semmelweis made doctors wash in chlorinated lime after autopsies and deaths fell to 1–2%. Yet many colleagues rejected the idea that a gentleman's hands could carry disease.

lead.en: A wave of uprisings sweeps across Europe

summary.en: The February Revolution in Paris toppled King Louis Philippe and set off uprisings across France, the German states, the Austrian Empire and Italy. Most were crushed, but serfdom was abolished in several lands and liberalism and nationalism became leading forces of the age.

lead.en: Marx and Engels: “Workers of the world, unite!”

summary.en: In February 1848 a pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, commissioned by the Communist League, appeared in London. The Manifesto described history as class struggle and predicted the fall of capitalism. It became one of the most influential political texts, inspiring socialist parties and the revolutions of the 20th century.

lead.en: Flakes in a mill race reshaped the American West

summary.en: On 24 January 1848 carpenter James Marshall spotted flakes of gold in the channel of Sutter's sawmill. The news spread worldwide, and within a few years some 300,000 fortune-seekers, the 'forty-niners', arrived from every continent. San Francisco grew from a village into a city of tens of thousands, and by 1850 California had become a state.

title.en: Phineas Gage and the iron rod

lead.en: An iron rod went through his head; he was talking within minutes

summary.en: Blasting rock for a railway, 25-year-old foreman Phineas Gage had a metre-long iron rod driven clean through his skull. He survived, was talking within minutes and lived almost 12 more years, and his case became an early lesson in how the frontal lobes shape personality.
